readings.title: Measuring air near a school
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Residents used portable sensors near a school gate. Their readings changed sharply when buses were waiting outside. The main obstacle was measurements taken at inconsistent times. Some volunteers sampled before the morning rush while others arrived after it. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a common timetable and location map. The group repeated readings at fixed points and noted weather and traffic conditions. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated consistent records showed the busiest period. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a regular published measurement schedule. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: environmental data needs a repeatable method. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in measuring air near a school, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Listening for noise after dark
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Neighbours complained about evening noise beside a delivery yard. Accounts differed because the loudest periods were brief. The main obstacle was reports without exact times or sources. General descriptions made it hard to distinguish deliveries from ordinary street activity. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a dated noise diary and site visits. Residents recorded times while staff observed the yard without identifying individual workers. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated one late delivery slot caused most disturbance. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a revised unloading window agreed with the operator. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: specific evidence supports fair solutions. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in listening for noise after dark, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A stream after heavy rain
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A student group noticed cloudy water in a small stream after storms. Its first samples were taken at different points each week. The main obstacle was samples that could not be compared reliably. A change in location might explain a result as easily as a change in water quality. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used fixed safe sampling locations. Teachers checked conditions, recorded rainfall and used appropriate supervision for every visit. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated rainfall timing shaped the observed pattern. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a log that links samples to weather conditions. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: a useful observation needs context. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in a stream after heavy rain, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Sharing a neighbourhood temperature map
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Volunteers measured heat on local streets. Their map seemed to show one park as the hottest place, surprising regular visitors. The main obstacle was readings taken in sun and shade without labels. Different surfaces and times of day had been mixed in one colour scale. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a review of measurement conditions. The team compared device placement, shade and timing before presenting the map again. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated the first map hid important differences. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced separate maps for comparable conditions. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: clear data presentation matters as much as collection. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in sharing a neighbourhood temperature map, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
When a community changes the neighbourhood environment programme, a short explanation can be as important as the change itself. People want to know what problem was noticed, how information was gathered and why one option was selected. For a project about environmental monitoring and community action, staff observed actual use rather than relying only on a drawing or an early promise. The evidence revealed an obstacle that was not obvious at first. Organizers made a limited adjustment and told residents when it would be reviewed. They also described the limits of the trial, because a small number of visits cannot represent every future situation. An honest account made the decision easier to question and improve.

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the local environment group suggesting a practical change to the neighbourhood environment programme. Describe who should be consulted, how the change could be tried, and when it should be reviewed.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the neighbourhood environment programme. People have noticed measurements taken at inconsistent times, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
